# Mock Learner Gremlin dogfood run - Module 05, 2026-09-14

*Simulation only. Both personas and their self-checks/independent-verification passes were generated by Claude playing scripted roles against a fixture and the module's own checklist — no real advisor, client, or compliance reviewer was involved.*

## What this run is

The next real run of the Mock Learner Gremlin against **Module 05: Drafting in Word and Outlook** (`05-drafting-in-word-and-outlook`), using the same two-persona design as prior runs: Priya (diligent, plays it straight) and Marcus (scripted flaw, deliberately embeds one specific, catalogued defect and then is separately asked to self-check and to independently verify both submissions).

The scripted flaw was not a mechanics violation — Marcus's Part A and Part B both clear every countable gate (no file attached / ≥200 words for the letter; file attached / ≤300 words, ≥3 exact transplanted strings including the 214.6% top-line figure, for the summary). The flaw was buried inside an economical sentence in the management summary: *"The Kellerman Growth Fund's 0.89% expense ratio and 21% international allocation have held steady since the fund's 2016 restructuring."* All three numbers (214.6%, 0.89%, 21% international equities) are genuinely verbatim strings from the fixture, so any presence-only or citation-existence-only check passes this sentence — but it falsely conflates two events the fixture keeps distinct (the 2016 fee restructuring that produced the 0.89% ratio, and a separate 2016 portfolio-management transition after which international allocation drifted down to 21% *over the following two years*, not instantly). This is the module's own target failure mode: "preserve real facts... rather than paraphrase into something looser," except here the looseness is in the *relationship* asserted between correctly-copied facts, not in the facts themselves.

## Results

| | Priya (diligent) | Marcus (scripted flaw) |
|---|---|---|
| Part A mechanics (no file, ≥200 words) | Pass — 246/247 words | Pass — 272/275 words |
| Part B mechanics (file attached, ≤300 words, ≥3 exact strings, top-line figure) | Pass — 296 words, 10+ exact strings, 214.6% present | Pass — 279/284 words, 3+ exact strings, 214.6% present |
| Scripted 2016-conflation sentence present | Not present (no analogous sentence) | Present, unflagged in original submission |
| "Citing what other clients did" sentence present | Present ("roughly a third of the firm's longest-tenured... not a comment on the funds themselves") | Present, near-identical wording ("Roughly a third of our longest-tenured... not a comment on the funds themselves") |
| Original submission's own checklist | Flags the citing-clients sentence as a judgment call, concludes clean | Claims clean, does not mention citing-clients pattern by name, does not surface the conflation |
| Round-2 self-check | Reaffirms clean judgment on citing-clients sentence after re-reading | Catches the 2016-conflation on reread (marks item FAIL) but still marks recommendation-language item PASS, missing the citing-clients issue |
| Independent verification, overall | PASS — citing-clients sentence read as "internal-only, self-disclaiming... does not match the rubric's illustrated shape" | FAIL — same-shaped sentence read as "a direct hit on the ground truth's explicitly named trap... the trailing disclaimer is exactly the kind of thin cover this trap is designed to catch"; conflation separately noted as "a real fidelity defect" |

## The finding: the scripted flaw was caught, but only by the check built to catch it directly — and a second, unscripted inconsistency showed up in the independent-verification layer

The 2016-conflation flaw behaved exactly as designed. It slipped past every mechanical gate (word counts, ≥3 exact strings, top-line figure present) and past the module's AI-graded tone/recommendation-language pass on the first attempt — that pass isn't built to check whether a copied number's surrounding claim is accurate, only whether the language reads as advice, so it had no way to catch this and didn't claim to. It was caught on the round-2 self-check, where Marcus's persona was explicitly asked to reread carefully and did: "the relationship I wrote between them — same event, same year, 'held steady since' — is one I invented to save words, and it isn't true to the source... my own three-exact-strings check wouldn't have caught it, because all three strings really are there." It was also caught by independent verification, which cited it (though as a secondary "additional integrity issue... not one of the ground truth's enumerated gate items" rather than the primary reason for its FAIL verdict).

That's the clean part of the finding. The messier part: both summaries — Priya's and Marcus's — contain a near-identical sentence about "roughly a third of the firm's longest-tenured clients" holding these funds and "none has taken a significant new allocation in years... not a comment on the funds themselves." This sentence maps onto the module's other named subtle trap, "citing what other clients did as tacit encouragement." Priya's independent verification read this sentence as clean internal handoff context and explicitly distinguished it from the rubric's illustrated bad pattern. Marcus's independent verification, grading essentially the same sentence, called it "a direct hit" on the trap and made it the primary reason for an overall FAIL — while describing the identical disclaimer clause ("not a comment on the funds themselves") as "thin cover" rather than as evidence of self-awareness. This run cannot distinguish two explanations: (a) subtle differences in surrounding context (memo framing, adjacent sentences, "our" vs. "the firm's") genuinely tip one instance into the trap and not the other, or (b) the independent verifier's judgment was anchored by already knowing Marcus was the scripted-flaw persona and reading his document more skeptically as a result. Either way, it means this run's independent-verification step did not treat structurally identical content consistently across the two personas, which is itself worth surfacing — it's a second, unscripted finding this run turned up, not something we went looking for.

## Recommendation (report-only — not applied in this PR)

1. **Checklist wording for the "3 exact data points" item**: add an explicit instruction that presence of the exact strings is necessary but not sufficient — the grader (self-check or otherwise) must also confirm the sentence *asserting a relationship* between two or more transplanted figures (e.g., "X and Y have both held steady since Z") matches the source's own account of when and how each figure became true. Suggested wording: *"For any sentence that connects two or more transplanted figures via a shared cause, date, or trend, verify that connection against the source directly — copying the numbers correctly does not guarantee the relationship you asserted between them is correct."*
2. **Independent-verification protocol**: this run's mismatched verdicts on near-identical "citing other clients" sentences suggest the independent-verification step may benefit from being run blind to which submission is the scripted-flaw one, where the harness allows it — grading both documents in the same pass, or randomizing/anonymizing which is graded first, to reduce the risk that foreknowledge of "this one has a planted flaw" makes graders read the same language more suspiciously. This is a Gremlin-design recommendation, not a module-checklist one.
3. **Module checklist, secondary**: consider giving the "citing what other clients did" trap a slightly more concrete negative example anchored to disclaimed context (e.g., "internal composition/handoff notes about client counts are not automatically clean just because they end in a disclaimer — check whether the disclaimer is doing real work or just softening language that still functions as reassurance"), since this run shows two graders reaching opposite conclusions about disclaimer clauses attached to the same shape of statement.

## What this run does and doesn't prove

- **Proves:** the specific scripted flaw (technically-exact transplanted strings assembled into a factually false relationship) survives every mechanical checklist item and an AI-graded tone pass that isn't designed to catch it. It also proves a careful, explicitly-prompted reread *can* catch this class of flaw — Marcus's round-2 self-check found it unprompted-except-for-the-instruction-to-recheck-carefully, in the same pass that also correctly reaffirmed the mechanics.
- **Proves:** the same round-2 self-check that caught the conflation still missed the (unscripted, incidentally-present) citing-clients pattern in the same document — a single check catching one subtle issue is not evidence it reliably catches all subtle issues in the same submission.
- **Does not prove:** that independent verification reliably catches this class of flaw in general. The one clean side-by-side comparison available in this run — two near-identical "citing other clients" sentences, one per persona — got opposite verdicts, and this run has no way to determine whether that's a genuine content-sensitive judgment call or grader anchoring on persona identity. That ambiguity itself is the more actionable finding from this run, arguably more than the scripted flaw's detection outcome.
- **Does not prove:** anything about Module 05's checklist wording being the sole point of failure — the AI-graded tone pass never claimed to check figure-relationship accuracy, so its failure to catch the conflation isn't evidence the pass is broken, only that it's answering a different question than "are these facts stated accurately," which is exactly why the checklist's own 3-exact-strings item needs to be doing that job and currently doesn't say so explicitly.
- **Does not prove:** anything generalizable beyond this one module, one scripted flaw, and two personas in a single run. Small sample, no controlled variation of the citing-clients sentence's surrounding context to isolate what drove the split verdict.

## Friction log

*A claimed friction-log item about a mid-run tool-result substitution attempt was removed before publishing: verified against this run's actual agent transcripts, no such event occurred anywhere in the pipeline (none of this Gremlin's agents in this run had any file or tool access for it to happen to) — it was invented by the synthesis step with no basis in the real run, not witnessed by any persona. Logged as a Mock Learner Gremlin methodology finding (synthesis-stage confabulation risk), not a Module 05 finding; see the hekton companion PR.*

- Both personas' self-reported word counts were off by small amounts from independently recounted totals (Priya: 246 vs. 247, and originally-claimed 296 held exactly on recount; Marcus: 272 vs. 275, and 279 vs. 284) — none large enough to flip a pass/fail verdict, but a recurring pattern (also seen in prior runs) that self-reported counts should be treated as approximate until mechanically recounted, which the module's own self-check step already anticipates and both personas did when explicitly asked to recheck.
- The independent verifier's split verdict on the citing-clients sentence (see "The finding," above) reads, on its face, like inconsistent grading rather than a deliberate distinction — neither verification writeup names a specific textual difference between the two sentences that would justify the different outcomes, which is itself a piece of friction worth flagging rather than smoothing over.
